core_knowledge.definition: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7), a terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, supplies the three anterior arm (flexor) compartment muscles — biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis — before continuing distally as a purely sensory nerve (the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) supplying skin over the lateral forearm; its course PIERCING THROUGH coracobrachialis is a distinctive, frequently tested anatomical detail, and its relative anatomical protection (compared to some other brachial plexus terminal branches) explains its relatively low injury rate in most upper limb trauma.

structure_anatomy.origin_and_course: Arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus (C5-C7), then characteristically PIERCES THROUGH the coracobrachialis muscle (a distinctive, specific anatomical detail — most nerves run alongside or deep to muscles, not directly through their substance) before running distally between biceps brachii and brachialis, supplying all three anterior arm compartment muscles along its course, then continuing as the purely sensory lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, emerging lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow.
structure_anatomy.muscles_supplied: Coracobrachialis (flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder), biceps brachii (flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm — its most powerful action combination occurring together, e.g. turning a screwdriver/corkscrew), and brachialis (the primary, most powerful pure elbow flexor, working effectively regardless of forearm position, unlike biceps whose flexion power is reduced in pronation).

clinical.relative_injury_protection: Compared to some other terminal brachial plexus branches (e.g. axillary nerve at the surgical neck of humerus, radial nerve at the spiral groove), the musculocutaneous nerve is relatively protected from common injury mechanisms, given its course piercing directly through and partially embedded within coracobrachialis muscle substance for part of its length — though it remains vulnerable to specific injury mechanisms including penetrating trauma, some surgical procedures in the axilla/proximal arm region (e.g. certain shoulder surgery approaches), and rarely from severe traction injuries to the brachial plexus.
clinical.isolated_lesion_findings: Isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury produces weakness of elbow flexion (though NOT complete loss, since brachioradialis — a radial nerve-supplied muscle — provides some elbow flexion contribution as a backup) and forearm supination (with supinator, a separate radial-nerve-supplied muscle, also contributing some residual supination capacity), PLUS sensory loss over the lateral forearm (the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm's territory) — a combination of motor and sensory findings in this specific distribution.

concept_blueprint.related_structures: The musculocutaneous nerve's transition from a purely MOTOR nerve (in the arm, supplying the three flexor compartment muscles) to a purely SENSORY nerve (in the forearm, as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) at a single continuous nerve trunk is a genuinely elegant example of a peripheral nerve's dual-phase identity — worth recognising as a specific, nameable transition point rather than assuming the nerve's entire course shares one uniform function.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Musculocutaneous nerve's course through coracobrachialis, anterior arm compartment supply, and its motor-to-sensory transition
mcqs.question: The musculocutaneous nerve has a distinctive anatomical relationship with which specific muscle, unusual compared to how most nerves relate to muscles?
options: It PIERCES THROUGH the substance of coracobrachialis, rather than running alongside or deep to it
It runs entirely superficial to all three muscles it supplies, with no direct muscular relationship
It originates FROM within triceps brachii muscle tissue itself
It has no distinctive relationship with any specific muscle along its course
mcqs.correct_answer: It PIERCES THROUGH the substance of coracobrachialis, rather than running alongside or deep to it

distractor_rationale.It runs entirely superficial to all thre: Understates the genuinely distinctive PIERCING relationship specifically with coracobrachialis — the nerve doesn't just run superficial to its target muscles.
distractor_rationale.It originates FROM within triceps brachi: Triceps brachii is a POSTERIOR compartment muscle (radial nerve territory), entirely unrelated to the musculocutaneous nerve's anterior compartment course and origin.
distractor_rationale.It has no distinctive relationship with: Denies the genuine, specifically distinctive, frequently tested piercing relationship with coracobrachialis.

explanation.core_concept: The musculocutaneous nerve piercing directly THROUGH coracobrachialis's muscle substance (rather than the more typical pattern of running alongside or deep to a muscle) is a genuinely distinctive, specifically named anatomical relationship, making it a favourite, precise detail for testing whether a nerve's course has been learned with genuine anatomical specificity.
explanation.why_correct: The musculocutaneous nerve characteristically PIERCES THROUGH the substance of coracobrachialis muscle — a distinctive anatomical relationship, since most nerves run alongside, superficial to, or deep to the muscles they pass near, rather than running directly through a muscle's own substance.

why_others_wrong.It runs entirely superficial to all thre: Understates the specific, distinctive PIERCING relationship with coracobrachialis specifically.
why_others_wrong.It originates FROM within triceps brachi: Triceps brachii is an entirely unrelated, posterior compartment muscle, with no relationship to the musculocutaneous nerve's course or origin.
why_others_wrong.It has no distinctive relationship with: Denies the genuine, specific, frequently tested coracobrachialis-piercing relationship.

high_yield_facts: Musculocutaneous nerve PIERCES coracobrachialis — a genuinely distinctive, specifically named anatomical relationship.
This piercing course is a favourite, precise exam detail testing whether the nerve's SPECIFIC course (not just its general territory) has been learned.
This is directly relevant to surgical anatomy in the axilla/proximal arm, where awareness of this piercing course helps avoid inadvertent nerve injury during dissection in this region.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Surgeons operating in the axilla or proximal arm (e.g. for certain shoulder procedures) must be aware of this piercing course, since the nerve's position within coracobrachialis muscle substance (rather than simply alongside it) has direct implications for surgical dissection technique and nerve preservation.
common_confusions: Assuming all peripheral nerves run either alongside or deep to their target muscles — the musculocutaneous nerve's PIERCING course through coracobrachialis specifically is a genuine, distinctive exception worth remembering precisely.
related_concepts: Anterior arm compartment muscle supply (this concept, other question) — coracobrachialis being one of the three muscles this nerve supplies
exam_traps: Don't confuse 'runs near' or 'runs deep to' with the SPECIFIC 'pierces through' relationship the musculocutaneous nerve has with coracobrachialis — this precise detail is exactly what distinguishes a careful answer from an approximate one.
explanation.memory_aid: Musculocutaneous nerve doesn't just walk past coracobrachialis — it walks straight THROUGH it.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This distinctive course is directly relevant to correctly identifying the nerve on dissection or in surgical anatomy contexts.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: The musculocutaneous nerve characteristically pierces through the substance of coracobrachialis muscle — a distinctive, specifically named anatomical relationship unlike the more typical pattern of nerves running alongside or deep to muscles.
explanation.source_reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, upper limb chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: State that the musculocutaneous nerve characteristically pierces through the coracobrachialis muscle.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Musculocutaneous nerve's course through coracobrachialis, anterior arm compartment supply, and its motor-to-sensory transition
mcqs.question: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies all three muscles of the anterior arm compartment. Which of the following is one of these three muscles?
options: Brachialis
Triceps brachii
Anconeus
Supinator

distractor_rationale.Triceps brachii: A POSTERIOR arm compartment muscle, supplied by the radial nerve — not part of the musculocutaneous nerve's anterior compartment territory.
distractor_rationale.Anconeus: A small posterior compartment muscle, also radial-nerve-supplied, unrelated to the musculocutaneous nerve.
distractor_rationale.Supinator: A forearm (not arm) muscle, supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve (radial nerve branch) — a different muscle, different compartment, and different nerve entirely.

explanation.core_concept: Brachialis, along with coracobrachialis and biceps brachii, forms the complete, specific three-muscle territory of the musculocutaneous nerve — brachialis specifically deserves recognition as the body's primary, most powerful PURE elbow flexor, distinct from biceps's combined flexion/supination role.
explanation.why_correct: Brachialis is one of the three anterior arm compartment muscles supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (alongside coracobrachialis and biceps brachii) — brachialis is specifically the primary, most powerful pure elbow flexor, working effectively regardless of forearm position.

why_others_wrong.Triceps brachii: A posterior compartment, radial-nerve-supplied muscle — not musculocutaneous nerve territory.
why_others_wrong.Anconeus: Also a posterior compartment, radial-nerve-supplied muscle.
why_others_wrong.Supinator: A forearm muscle (not an arm muscle), supplied by a radial nerve branch — different compartment, different nerve entirely.

high_yield_facts: Musculocutaneous nerve's three muscles: coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, BRACHIALIS.
Brachialis = the primary, most powerful PURE elbow flexor (works regardless of forearm position) — distinct from biceps, whose flexion power is somewhat reduced in the pronated position.
All three muscles are ANTERIOR arm compartment (flexor) muscles — contrast with the posterior compartment (triceps, anconeus), entirely different territory, radial nerve supplied.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Testing pure elbow flexion strength (particularly with the forearm in a neutral or pronated position, minimising biceps's specific contribution) helps isolate brachialis function specifically, relevant to assessing musculocutaneous nerve integrity.
common_confusions: Confusing anterior (musculocutaneous nerve) and posterior (radial nerve) arm compartment muscles — triceps, anconeus, and supinator are all radial-nerve-supplied, genuinely different territory from the musculocutaneous nerve's specific three-muscle anterior compartment supply.
related_concepts: Coracobrachialis-piercing course (this concept, other question) — the SAME muscle the nerve pierces through is also one of the three it supplies
exam_traps: Don't include any posterior compartment muscle (triceps, anconeus) or forearm muscle (supinator) in the musculocutaneous nerve's territory — its supply is specifically limited to the three ANTERIOR ARM compartment muscles.
explanation.memory_aid: Musculocutaneous nerve's muscles: Coracobrachialis, Biceps, Brachialis — all three anterior arm 'C-B-B' flexors.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This muscle territory is the direct anatomical basis for the isolated nerve lesion findings covered elsewhere in this chapter.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Brachialis, along with coracobrachialis and biceps brachii, is one of the three anterior arm compartment muscles supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve — distinct from the radial-nerve-supplied posterior compartment (triceps, anconeus) and forearm (supinator) muscles.
explanation.source_reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, upper limb chapter.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Musculocutaneous nerve's course through coracobrachialis, anterior arm compartment supply, and its motor-to-sensory transition
mcqs.question: The musculocutaneous nerve has a genuinely distinctive 'dual-phase' identity along its course. Describe this transition, and name the nerve's terminal sensory continuation.
options: The nerve is purely MOTOR in the arm (supplying the three anterior compartment muscles), then continues distally as a purely SENSORY nerve — the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying skin over the lateral forearm
The nerve is purely sensory throughout its entire course, with no motor component at any point
The nerve is purely motor throughout its entire course, terminating without any sensory continuation at all
The nerve alternates between motor and sensory function multiple times along its course, with no single, clean transition point
mcqs.correct_answer: The nerve is purely MOTOR in the arm (supplying the three anterior compartment muscles), then continues distally as a purely SENSORY nerve — the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, supplying skin over the lateral forearm

distractor_rationale.The nerve is purely sensory throughout i: Denies the nerve's genuine, substantial motor role in the arm (supplying three muscles) before its sensory continuation.
distractor_rationale.The nerve is purely motor throughout its: Denies the nerve's genuine sensory continuation (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) after completing its motor territory in the arm.
distractor_rationale.The nerve alternates between motor and s: Overcomplicates the actual pattern — there is a single, clean, well-defined transition (motor in the arm, then purely sensory from the elbow region distally), not multiple alternating phases.

explanation.core_concept: Recognising the musculocutaneous nerve as having a clean, single 'dual-phase' identity — entirely motor proximally, entirely sensory distally — is a genuinely elegant way to understand this nerve as a coherent, single continuous structure with two sequential functional roles, rather than needing to memorise its motor and sensory territories as unrelated facts.
explanation.why_correct: The musculocutaneous nerve is purely MOTOR throughout its course in the arm, supplying the three anterior compartment muscles (coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis) along the way. After completing this motor territory, near the elbow, it continues as a purely SENSORY nerve — the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm — emerging lateral to the biceps tendon and supplying skin over the lateral aspect of the forearm.

why_others_wrong.The nerve is purely sensory throughout i: Denies the substantial, well-established motor territory (three muscles) in the arm.
why_others_wrong.The nerve is purely motor throughout its: Denies the genuine sensory continuation as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
why_others_wrong.The nerve alternates between motor and s: Overcomplicates the actual, single, clean transition pattern.

high_yield_facts: Musculocutaneous nerve: PURELY MOTOR in the arm (3 muscles) → PURELY SENSORY distally (lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm, lateral forearm skin).

This single, clean transition point (near the elbow, lateral to the biceps tendon) is what makes this nerve's dual identity coherent and predictable, rather than requiring separate memorisation of its motor and sensory facts.

This dual-phase pattern directly explains why isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury produces BOTH motor (elbow flexion/supination weakness) AND sensory (lateral forearm numbness) findings TOGETHER, covered elsewhere in this chapter.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Understanding this transition helps correctly interpret clinical findings — motor weakness alone (without lateral forearm sensory loss) would argue against a musculocutaneous nerve lesion specifically, since a genuine lesion of this nerve should affect BOTH its motor and sensory territories together, given their shared single nerve trunk origin.
common_confusions: Assuming a nerve's function must be uniformly either 'motor' or 'sensory' throughout its entire course — the musculocutaneous nerve is a clean example of a nerve with a genuine, single transition from one functional identity to the other along its length.
related_concepts: Anterior arm compartment muscle supply (this concept, other question) — the motor phase of this nerve's course
Isolated lesion findings (this concept, other question) — directly reflecting BOTH phases together
exam_traps: Don't assume the musculocutaneous nerve is 'just a motor nerve' or 'just a sensory nerve' — actively recall its genuine DUAL identity, with a clean transition point near the elbow.
explanation.memory_aid: Motor in the arm, sensory in the forearm — one nerve, two clean jobs, one clear handoff point near the elbow.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This dual-phase understanding directly explains the combined motor-and-sensory findings in isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury, covered elsewhere in this chapter.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: The musculocutaneous nerve is purely motor in the arm (supplying coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis) before continuing distally as a purely sensory nerve — the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm — a clean, single transition point worth recognising as this nerve's genuine dual-phase identity.
explanation.source_reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, upper limb chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: Explain the musculocutaneous nerve's transition from purely motor (in the arm) to purely sensory (lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm) function.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Musculocutaneous nerve's course through coracobrachialis, anterior arm compartment supply, and its motor-to-sensory transition
mcqs.question: A patient sustains an isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury from a penetrating axillary injury. Examination shows weakness (but not complete loss) of elbow flexion and forearm supination, plus numbness over the lateral forearm. Why is elbow flexion weakened rather than completely absent, despite this nerve supplying the primary elbow flexors?
options: Brachioradialis, a RADIAL-nerve-supplied muscle, provides a backup contribution to elbow flexion, preventing complete loss despite musculocutaneous nerve injury affecting its own primary flexors (biceps, brachialis)
Elbow flexion would actually be completely, totally absent with this injury, and this vignette's description is clinically inaccurate
The musculocutaneous nerve has no role in elbow flexion at all, making this finding entirely unrelated to the described injury
Triceps brachii compensates for the lost flexors by paradoxically assisting with flexion in this specific injury pattern
mcqs.correct_answer: Brachioradialis, a RADIAL-nerve-supplied muscle, provides a backup contribution to elbow flexion, preventing complete loss despite musculocutaneous nerve injury affecting its own primary flexors (biceps, brachialis)

distractor_rationale.Elbow flexion would actually be complete: Denies the genuine, well-established backup contribution from brachioradialis, which is precisely why complete loss doesn't occur despite losing the nerve's own primary flexor muscles.
distractor_rationale.The musculocutaneous nerve has no role i: Directly contradicts the well-established fact that biceps brachii and brachialis (both musculocutaneous-nerve-supplied) are the PRIMARY elbow flexors.
distractor_rationale.Triceps brachii compensates for the lost: Triceps brachii is specifically an ELBOW EXTENSOR, not a flexor — it wouldn't compensate for lost flexion function; this option describes an anatomically implausible compensatory mechanism.

explanation.core_concept: This vignette demonstrates a genuinely important principle — even when a nerve supplies the PRIMARY muscles for a given movement, a backup contribution from a DIFFERENT nerve's muscle can prevent complete functional loss, explaining why isolated nerve lesions often produce partial rather than complete deficits for movements with more than one contributing muscle.
explanation.why_correct: Brachioradialis, a forearm muscle supplied by the RADIAL nerve (not the musculocutaneous nerve), provides a genuine backup contribution to elbow flexion. Even with complete musculocutaneous nerve injury eliminating biceps brachii and brachialis's contribution (the PRIMARY elbow flexors), brachioradialis's intact, radial-nerve-supplied function prevents COMPLETE loss of elbow flexion, explaining the vignette's described WEAKNESS (not complete absence) of this movement — directly analogous to how supinator (also radial-nerve-supplied) provides some residual supination capacity despite loss of biceps's own supination contribution.

why_others_wrong.Elbow flexion would actually be complete: Denies the genuine backup contribution from brachioradialis, which is exactly why complete loss doesn't occur.
why_others_wrong.The musculocutaneous nerve has no role i: Directly contradicts biceps brachii and brachialis's well-established roles as the PRIMARY elbow flexors, both musculocutaneous-nerve-supplied.
why_others_wrong.Triceps brachii compensates for the lost: Triceps is an elbow EXTENSOR, anatomically incapable of compensating for lost flexion function.

high_yield_facts: Isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury → WEAK (not absent) elbow flexion, since brachioradialis (radial nerve) provides backup contribution.
Similarly → weak (not absent) supination, since supinator (also radial nerve) provides some residual capacity.

This pattern (partial, not complete, loss) reflects a general principle: movements with MULTIPLE contributing muscles from DIFFERENT nerves rarely show complete loss from a single isolated nerve injury — worth recognising as a transferable concept beyond just this specific nerve.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Recognising this partial-loss pattern helps correctly localise and characterise the SPECIFIC nerve injury (isolated musculocutaneous, versus a more extensive injury affecting multiple nerves), directly relevant to prognosis discussion and surgical/rehabilitation planning.
common_confusions: Assuming a nerve supplying the 'primary' muscles for a movement must be solely and completely responsible for that movement — genuine backup contributions from OTHER nerves' muscles (like brachioradialis here) often prevent complete functional loss, even with total loss of the primary nerve's own contribution.
related_concepts: Muscle supply (this concept, other question) — establishing biceps/brachialis as the PRIMARY (not sole) elbow flexors
Motor-to-sensory transition (this concept, other question) — explaining the accompanying sensory finding in this same vignette
exam_traps: Don't assume 'primary muscle for a movement' means 'only possible contributor' — actively consider whether OTHER muscles, potentially supplied by different nerves, could provide backup function even after the primary nerve's contribution is lost.
explanation.memory_aid: Biceps and brachialis do the heavy lifting for elbow flexion, but brachioradialis (a different nerve's muscle) can still pitch in and keep some flexion going.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This vignette directly synthesises the muscle supply and motor-to-sensory transition facts established elsewhere in this chapter into a complete, realistic clinical presentation.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury produces WEAKNESS (not complete loss) of elbow flexion, because brachioradialis (a radial-nerve-supplied muscle) provides a genuine backup contribution despite loss of the nerve's own primary flexors (biceps brachii, brachialis).
explanation.source_reference: Standard clinical neuroanatomy references on isolated musculocutaneous nerve injury.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Musculocutaneous nerve's course through coracobrachialis, anterior arm compartment supply, and its motor-to-sensory transition
mcqs.question: How does biceps brachii's contribution to elbow flexion differ from brachialis's contribution, particularly regarding forearm position?
options: Brachialis is the primary, POSITION-INDEPENDENT elbow flexor (consistent power regardless of forearm position); biceps brachii's flexion power is POSITION-DEPENDENT, strongest when the forearm is supinated
Both muscles contribute identically to elbow flexion regardless of forearm position, with no meaningful difference between them
Biceps brachii is the primary, position-independent flexor, while brachialis's flexion power varies significantly with forearm position — the reverse of the correct distinction
Neither muscle contributes meaningfully to elbow flexion; this function is performed entirely by brachioradialis instead
mcqs.correct_answer: Brachialis is the primary, POSITION-INDEPENDENT elbow flexor (consistent power regardless of forearm position); biceps brachii's flexion power is POSITION-DEPENDENT, strongest when the forearm is supinated

distractor_rationale.Neither muscle contributes meaningfully: Denies the well-established primary roles of both muscles.

explanation.core_concept: Comparing biceps brachii and brachialis's elbow flexion contributions directly reinforces brachialis's status as the primary, position-independent flexor — a genuinely useful distinction for predicting exactly how flexion strength varies with forearm position, and for understanding why isolated injury patterns can affect these two muscles' contributions differently.
explanation.why_correct: Biceps brachii's flexion power is position-dependent — it flexes the elbow most powerfully when the forearm is SUPINATED (since biceps is also the primary supinator, and its mechanical advantage for flexion is greatest in this position), with reduced flexion contribution when the forearm is pronated. Brachialis, by contrast, is the primary PURE elbow flexor, working with consistent, powerful contribution REGARDLESS of forearm position (supinated, neutral, or pronated) — making it the more reliable, position-independent flexor of the two.

why_others_wrong.Both muscles contribute identically to e: Denies a genuine, well-established difference in how each muscle's flexion contribution varies with forearm position.
why_others_wrong.Biceps brachii is the primary, position-: Directly reverses which muscle has position-independent versus position-dependent flexion power.
why_others_wrong.Neither muscle contributes meaningfully: Denies the well-established, primary roles of both biceps brachii and brachialis in elbow flexion — brachioradialis provides a secondary, backup contribution, not the primary flexion function.

high_yield_facts: Brachialis: PRIMARY, POSITION-INDEPENDENT elbow flexor — consistent power regardless of forearm position.
Biceps brachii: flexion power is POSITION-DEPENDENT, strongest when the forearm is supinated (reflecting its dual role as flexor AND supinator).
This distinction is why clinical testing sometimes specifically assesses flexion with the forearm in different positions to help isolate/emphasise each muscle's relative contribution.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Understanding this position-dependent difference is relevant to physical therapy/rehabilitation exercise design (e.g. targeting brachialis specifically via flexion exercises performed in pronation, since biceps's contribution is reduced in that position) and to correctly interpreting elbow flexion strength testing in different forearm positions during clinical examination.
common_confusions: Assuming biceps brachii and brachialis contribute identically to elbow flexion regardless of forearm position — biceps's flexion power genuinely varies with position (strongest in supination), while brachialis remains the more consistent, position-independent flexor.
related_concepts: Muscle supply (this concept, other question) — establishing both muscles as musculocutaneous-nerve-supplied
Brachioradialis backup contribution (this concept, the clinical vignette question) — a THIRD muscle's contribution to flexion, from a different nerve
exam_traps: When a vignette specifies elbow flexion testing in a SPECIFIC forearm position (supinated vs pronated), use this position-dependent distinction to correctly interpret which muscle's contribution is being emphasised or isolated.
explanation.memory_aid: Brachialis flexes the same no matter what the forearm does; biceps flexes best when it's also busy supinating.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This distinction directly complements the muscle supply and brachioradialis backup facts established elsewhere in this chapter, completing the full picture of elbow flexion's multiple contributing muscles.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Brachialis is the primary, position-independent elbow flexor, while biceps brachii's flexion contribution is position-dependent, strongest when the forearm is supinated — both musculocutaneous-nerve-supplied, but with genuinely different mechanical behaviour.
explanation.source_reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, upper limb chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: Contrast brachialis's position-independent elbow flexion with biceps brachii's position-dependent flexion contribution.
